evidence.claim: From a former lumber town through volcanic country to Tule Lake.
evidence.quote: Beginning in McCloud, the Modoc Volcanic Scenic Byway travels through some unique volcanic scenery in the eastern portion of the Forest on its way to Medicine Lake, Lava Beds National Monument, and Tule Lake.

evidence.claim: a former lumber town
evidence.quote: A lumber mill was built by the McCloud River Lumber Company

evidence.claim: The Modoc Volcanic Scenic Byway runs from McCloud through volcanic country toward Medicine Lake, Lava Beds National Monument and Tule Lake.
evidence.quote: Beginning in McCloud, the Modoc Volcanic Scenic Byway travels through some unique volcanic scenery in the eastern portion of the Forest on its way to Medicine Lake, Lava Beds National Monument, and Tule Lake.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service calls it the Modoc Volcanic National Scenic Byway and identifies sections of Highway 89 out of McCloud and a road northeast to Medicine Lake.
evidence.quote: Modoc Volcanic National Scenic Byway Incorporates parts of Highway 89 out of McCloud and Highway 49 northeast to Medicine Lake.

evidence.claim: Snow closes the route around November, depending on snowfall.
evidence.quote: Snow shuts this route down around November depending on the amount of snowfall.

evidence.claim: At McCloud, moving timber once depended on getting over the hills. A lumber mill established in 1892 failed because hauling lumber by oxen proved difficult.
evidence.quote: A. F. Friday George erected a lumber mill here in 1892. Difficulty hauling lumber over hills by oxen caused the business to fail.

evidence.claim: The McCloud River Railroad Company, founded in 1895, enabled lumber transport from the region.
evidence.quote: The McCloud River Railroad Company was founded in 1895, enabling the transport of lumber from the region.

evidence.claim: The later McCloud River Lumber Company mill supplied homes with electricity and steam heat as well as processing lumber.
evidence.quote: A lumber mill was built by the McCloud River Lumber Company, and electricity and steam heat for homes in McCloud was supplied by the mill.

evidence.claim: Start at McCloud on Mount Shasta’s southern slope.
evidence.quote: McCloud is located on the southern slope of Mount Shasta.

evidence.claim: The drive leads to Medicine Lake, then Lava Beds National Monument, before reaching Tule Lake.
evidence.quote: Beginning in McCloud, the Modoc Volcanic Scenic Byway travels through some unique volcanic scenery in the eastern portion of the Forest on its way to Medicine Lake, Lava Beds National Monument, and Tule Lake.

evidence.claim: Nearby Tulelake takes its name from the lake.
evidence.quote: The town is named after nearby Tule Lake.

evidence.claim: In McCloud, the lumber mill once reached into the home: it supplied electricity and steam heat to the company town’s houses.
evidence.quote: A lumber mill was built by the McCloud River Lumber Company, and electricity and steam heat for homes in McCloud was supplied by the mill.

evidence.claim: The mill was sold to U.S. Plywood in 1963, and the company homes passed to private owners in 1965.
evidence.quote: The mill was sold in 1963 to U.S. Plywood, and in 1965, company homes in McCloud were transferred to private owners.

evidence.claim: The McCloud Community Services District was formed to oversee utilities and public services.
evidence.quote: The McCloud Community Services District was formed to oversee utilities, library services, and police and fire protection.

evidence.claim: The mill closed in 1979, reopened the following year and closed again in 2002.
evidence.quote: The lumber mill closed in 1979, re-opened in 1980, and closed in 2002.

evidence.claim: Snow closes this route around November, depending on snowfall. Snow depths prevent vehicle travel except by snowmobile or snow cat.
evidence.quote: Snow shuts this route down around November depending on the amount of snowfall. Snow depth is prohibitive to all vehicular travel excluding snowmobiles and snow cats.

evidence.claim: A National Park Service marker identifies the former military cemetery at Guillem’s Graveyard in Lava Beds National Monument.
evidence.quote: A historical marker is at the site of the former Guillem's Graveyard on Hill Road, one mile South of Rim Road, in Lava Beds National Monument. The marker was placed there by National Park Service.

evidence.claim: Camp Guillem served as the U.S. Army command post during the Modoc War of 1872–1873.
evidence.quote: Camp Guillem was the U.S. Army command post for the Modoc War

evidence.claim: Modoc people defended their land against Army troops.
evidence.quote: A small group of Modoc defended their land

evidence.claim: Soldiers killed in the war were buried here, then reburied at Fort Klamath or the Presidio of San Francisco.
evidence.quote: The other 50 were later re-interred in a cemetery at Fort Klamath or Presidio of San Francisco in 1885, the Graveyard now has no bodies.

evidence.claim: No bodies remain in the graveyard. The marker stands on Hill Road, one mile south of Rim Road.
evidence.quote:
the Graveyard now has no bodies.
A historical marker is at the site of the former Guillem's Graveyard on Hill Road, one mile South of Rim Road

evidence.claim: The National Park Service marker marks a former cemetery whose burials were moved elsewhere.

evidence.claim: Tulelake’s first public land auction took place on April 15, 1931. More than 100 lots sold, at prices ranging from $65 to $350.
evidence.quote: The first public auction of Tulelake land parcels took place on April 15, 1931. Over 100 lots were sold for prices ranging from $65 to $350.

evidence.claim: Incorporation followed in 1937.
evidence.quote: In 1937, the city was incorporated.

evidence.claim: The town takes its name from nearby Tule Lake and sits near the Siskiyou–Modoc county line, at the northwestern corner of the Great Basin and Range.
evidence.quote: Tulelake is located near the Siskiyou-Modoc County line, at the northwestern corner of the Great Basin and Range.

evidence.claim: The town takes its name from nearby Tule Lake
evidence.quote: The town is named after nearby Tule Lake.

evidence.claim: McCloud occupies Mount Shasta’s southern slope, with part of its downtown listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: McCloud is located on the southern slope of Mount Shasta.

evidence.claim: with part of its downtown listed on the National Register of Historic Places.
evidence.quote: A portion of downtown McCloud is listed on the National Register of Historic Places.

evidence.quote: The McCloud River Railroad Company was founded in 1895, enabling the transport of lumber from the region.

flags: The Forest Service uses “National Scenic Byway”; material identifies a National Forest Scenic Byway. No designation date or rationale is supplied. Preserve the agency’s name without claiming an FHWA designation.
Cache has little road character and no construction or campaign history. Intro uses McCloud transport history and stays below 200 words; no grades, travel time or volcanic geology invented.
The Forest Service calls the road northeast to Medicine Lake “Highway 49”; omit that number because its road-system identity is not established.
Driving order is McCloud to Tulelake, reversing the material’s increasing strip miles. All three current moments and their coordinates are retained.

Guillem’s Graveyard cache conflicts on cemetery founding/opening chronology and war duration. Omit those cemetery dates and numerical casualty claims. No tribal or primary war history is cached; keep the account limited and measured.

Tulelake moment is short because the supported auction-to-incorporation story is simple. Changed the current claim that Tulelake “began” in 1931 to the narrower supported first public auction. Other reused current facts are supported.
